title: The Book of the Watchers
bigQuestion: How did 1 Enoch retell the short story in Genesis 6, and why did Michael Heiser think Genesis 6 was answering the stories of Babylon?

story.title: One Line Becomes a Chapter
story.kicker: A student reads Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch 6 side by side and notices how much the second one adds.
paragraphs: Maya had a project for her history class: compare two ancient texts about the same event. Her teacher had suggested Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch 6. Maya opened both on her phone, one in each half of the screen. On the left was Genesis in the King James Version. On the right was R. H. Charles's 1917 translation of 1 Enoch.

Genesis 6:1–4 took her less than a minute to read. The sons of God saw that human women were beautiful and married them. The Nephilim were on the earth in those days. Their children became famous mighty men of old. Then the story moved straight on to Noah and the flood. There were no names, no places and no reasons.

The Enoch side kept going. It named a leader called Semjaza. It said the heavenly beings made a promise together on a mountain called Hermon. It counted them: two hundred. It listed the names of their chief leaders. Then, in the next chapters, it told what they taught people and what happened to the earth.

Maya drew a line from each verse in Genesis to the parts of Enoch that expanded it. One short phrase in Genesis became many verses in Enoch. She wrote in her notebook: "Genesis leaves a gap. Enoch fills it in." Then she wrote a question she wanted to answer: "Why would someone fill it in like this?"

That is the kind of question scholars ask too. Michael Heiser spent years studying it. His answer, in his book Reversing Hermon (2017), took him far from Jerusalem, to the very old stories of ancient Babylon.
story.think: When one text is short and another retells it at length, what can you learn by comparing them? What should you be careful not to assume?

lessons.title: Four Short Verses
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 6:1–4 tells, very briefly, of the sons of God, human women and the Nephilim just before the flood.
reading: Genesis 6:1–4 comes right before the story of Noah. People were growing in number. The *sons of God* saw that the daughters of humans were beautiful, and they took wives. Then God said that humans would live 120 years. The passage ends by mentioning the *Nephilim* and the mighty men of old.

The passage is short and puzzling. Who are the sons of God? The Hebrew phrase is bene ha'elohim. In Job 1:6 and 38:7 the same kind of phrase clearly names heavenly beings. Heiser argued that Genesis 6 uses it the same way. In his reading, heavenly beings crossed a line God had set between heaven and earth.

Who are the Nephilim? The Hebrew word is not fully clear. Some connect it to a verb meaning "to fall." When Jewish scholars translated Genesis into Greek, in the *Septuagint*, they used the word gigantes, meaning giants. That is why the King James Version says "there were giants in the earth in those days."

words.d: in Hebrew bene ha'elohim; in Job 1:6 and 38:7, heavenly beings; in Genesis 6:2, readers debate who they are
a Hebrew word in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33 whose exact meaning is debated; the Septuagint translated it as giants
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun around the 200s BCE

look.title: Genesis 6:2
look.text: That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.
look.prompt: What does this verse tell you, and what does it leave out? List two questions a reader might ask after reading it.

check.q: Where else does a phrase like "sons of God" clearly name heavenly beings?
check.why: In Job 1:6 and 38:7 the sons of God are heavenly beings, which Heiser used to read Genesis 6.

check.q: How did the Septuagint translate the word Nephilim?
check.why: The Greek Septuagint used gigantes, which is why the King James Version says giants.

check.q: Where does Genesis 6:1–4 come in the story of Genesis?
choices: At the creation of the world
Right before the story of Noah and the flood
check.why: Genesis 6:1–4 comes just before the flood story that begins with Noah.

lessons.title: Enoch Fills the Gap
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch 6–11 expands Genesis 6:1–4 into a longer story with names, numbers, a place and consequences.
reading: The Book of the Watchers retells Genesis 6 at length. In 1 Enoch the heavenly beings are called *Watchers*. The name also appears in Daniel 4, where a watcher, a holy one, comes down from heaven. In 1 Enoch the Watchers who came down are heavenly beings who leave their proper place.

Genesis 6:2 says the sons of God took wives. 1 Enoch 6–8 adds a leader, an oath, a mountain, a number and a list of names. It adds what they taught. It adds what happened to the earth. Then chapters 9–11 tell how heaven responded. This kind of retelling is called an *expansion*.

Scholars debate which came first. Most think Genesis 6 is older and 1 Enoch expands it. A few have suggested that both draw on an even older tradition. Either way, reading them side by side shows how Jewish writers in the Second Temple period understood Genesis 6.

words.d: in 1 Enoch, heavenly beings, especially those who came down to earth; the word also appears in Daniel 4
a retelling that adds details, names and scenes to a shorter earlier text

look.title: Side by Side
look.text: Genesis 6:2 (paraphrased): the sons of God saw human women and married them. 1 Enoch 6 (paraphrased): two hundred heavenly beings, led by Semjaza, agreed together to take human wives. Semjaza worried he alone would be blamed, so they all swore an oath on Mount Hermon.
look.prompt: List three details 1 Enoch adds that Genesis does not have. Why might a writer add a leader, a number and a place?

check.q: What does 1 Enoch call the heavenly beings who came down?
check.why: 1 Enoch calls them Watchers, a name also used for a heavenly being in Daniel 4.

check.q: What is an expansion?
choices: A retelling that adds details to a shorter, earlier text
check.why: 1 Enoch 6–11 is an expansion because it adds names, places and scenes to Genesis 6.

check.q: Which is something 1 Enoch adds that Genesis 6 does not include?
check.why: Only 1 Enoch 6 mentions an oath sworn on Mount Hermon.

lessons.title: Other Readings of Genesis 6
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser read the sons of God in Genesis 6 as heavenly beings; other readers see them as men from Seth's line or as kings.
reading: Heiser argued that the sons of God in Genesis 6 are heavenly beings. He pointed to Job, to the Septuagint and to 1 Enoch. He noted that 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 seem to know this reading. Many Jewish writers in the Second Temple period read the passage this way too.

Later, other readings grew popular. Many Christian writers, including Augustine, read the sons of God as godly men from the family of Seth, Adam's son. In this view the daughters of men came from Cain's family. Genesis 6 then describes two human families mixing. This is often called the *Sethite view*.

Some ancient Jewish interpreters read the sons of God as rulers or nobles. In that view, powerful men took any women they wanted. That is sometimes called the royal view. Each reading tries to fit the passage with the rest of the Bible. Heiser gave reasons for his view and explained why he found the others less convincing.

words.d: the reading that the sons of God in Genesis 6 were men from Seth's family line
the reading that the sons of God in Genesis 6 were kings or powerful rulers
a person who explains what a text means

look.title: Three Readings, One Verse
look.text: Reading A: the sons of God are heavenly beings who crossed into the human world (Heiser, Second Temple Jewish writers). Reading B: they are men from Seth's line marrying women from Cain's line (Augustine and many later Christians). Reading C: they are kings who took whatever they wanted (some Jewish interpreters).
look.prompt: Pick one reading. What evidence from Genesis, Job or 1 Enoch would its supporters point to? What question might its critics ask?

check.q: In the Sethite view, who are the sons of God?
choices: Men from the family line of Seth
check.why: The Sethite view, held by Augustine and many later Christians, reads them as men from Seth's line.

check.q: Which reading of Genesis 6 did Heiser hold?
choices: The sons of God were kings
The sons of God were men from Seth's line
The passage is only a poem
The sons of God were heavenly beings
check.why: Heiser argued the sons of God were heavenly beings, as in Job and 1 Enoch.

check.q: What is the royal view of Genesis 6?
choices: That the sons of God were powerful rulers
That the Nephilim were kings of Egypt
check.why: Some Jewish interpreters read the sons of God as rulers or nobles.

lessons.title: Two Hundred on the Mountain
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch 6 says two hundred Watchers, led by Shemihazah, swore an oath together on Mount Hermon in the days of Jared.
reading: 1 Enoch 6 names the leader of the Watchers. Charles's translation spells his name Semjaza. Many scholars write it *Shemihazah*, closer to the Aramaic. He fears he alone will be blamed. So all the Watchers swear an oath together, binding each other to the plan.

The book says there were two hundred of them. They came down in the days of Jared, Enoch's father. The Hebrew name Jared sounds like the verb yarad, "to go down." They came down on *Mount Hermon*. The book links the name Hermon to a Hebrew word for a solemn oath or ban.

Mount Hermon is a real mountain. It rises about 9,200 feet at the north edge of ancient Israel, on today's border of Lebanon and Syria. It is often covered with snow. Heiser gave Mount Hermon a central place in his book Reversing Hermon (2017), because this story begins there.

words.d: in 1 Enoch 6, the leader of the Watchers; Charles's translation spells it Semjaza
a mountain of about 9,200 feet at the north of ancient Israel; in 1 Enoch 6 the Watchers swear their oath there
a serious promise, often made with a call for punishment if it is broken

look.title: The Oath on Hermon
look.text: The Watchers were two hundred in all. They came down in the days of Jared onto the top of Mount Hermon. They named the mountain Hermon because there they swore an oath and bound themselves together.
look.cite: 1 Enoch 6:6, in R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917), paraphrased
look.prompt: The book explains a place name with a story. Why might an ancient writer connect a famous mountain to this event?

check.q: Who leads the Watchers in 1 Enoch 6?
check.why: 1 Enoch 6 names Shemihazah, spelled Semjaza by Charles, as their leader.

check.q: Why does the book mention the days of Jared?
choices: Jared's name sounds like the Hebrew verb "to go down"
check.why: The name Jared echoes yarad, "to go down," fitting the Watchers' descent.

check.q: Where is Mount Hermon?
choices: At the north edge of ancient Israel, near today's Lebanon and Syria
On the shore of the Dead Sea
check.why: Mount Hermon rises about 9,200 feet at the north edge of ancient Israel.

lessons.title: What the Watchers Taught
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch 7–8 says the Watchers taught people forbidden knowledge, such as weapon-making, cosmetics, sorcery and star-reading.
reading: In 1 Enoch the Watchers do more than marry. They teach. Chapter 8 names *Azazel*, also spelled Asael. He teaches people to work metal and to make swords, knives, shields and armor. He also teaches jewelry-making, makeup for the eyes and the use of colored dyes.

Other Watchers teach other things. Shemihazah teaches charms and the cutting of roots. Some teach how to read signs in the stars, the moon and the sun. In the book's view, this knowledge was given before people were ready. It spread harm, because weapons made fighting easier.

The story is not saying that metal, jewelry or learning are bad in themselves. The book's worry is about knowledge given the wrong way, by the wrong teachers, for the wrong reasons. Scholars call this theme *forbidden knowledge*. Many ancient stories, from Greece to Mesopotamia, ask where human skills came from.

words.d: in 1 Enoch 8, a Watcher who teaches metalwork, weapons and cosmetics; also spelled Asael; the name also appears in Leviticus 16
a story theme in which skills or secrets are given to people by those who should not have given them

look.title: Where Did Skills Come From?
look.text: In the Greek story, Prometheus gives fire to humans against the will of Zeus. In 1 Enoch 8, Azazel teaches metalwork and weapons. In Genesis 4:22, a man named Tubal-cain is the first worker of bronze and iron, with no heavenly teacher mentioned.
look.prompt: Compare the three. How is each one explaining where a human skill came from? What does each seem to think about that skill?

check.q: In 1 Enoch 8, what does Azazel teach?
check.why: 1 Enoch 8 says Azazel taught metalwork, weapons, jewelry and eye makeup.

check.q: What is the theme of forbidden knowledge?
choices: Skills or secrets given by those who should not have given them
check.why: In 1 Enoch the Watchers' teaching is a clear example of forbidden knowledge.

check.q: Why does 1 Enoch see the Watchers' teaching as harmful?
choices: Because the teaching was in Greek
Because it was given the wrong way and spread harm, such as easier fighting
Because people already knew it all
check.why: The book's worry is about knowledge given wrongly, which helped spread harm on earth.

lessons.title: Giants and a Hurting Earth
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch 7 says the Watchers' children were giants who used up the earth's food and harmed people and animals.
reading: 1 Enoch 7 says the Watchers' wives had children who grew into giants. The book links them to the Nephilim of Genesis 6. The giants ate everything people had grown. When the food ran out, they turned against people and creatures. The book describes the earth as suffering under them.

The story's main point is not the giants' size. It is how the world went wrong. In the book, the earth itself is like a person crying out for help. Violence spreads, and people call to heaven. This helps explain why, in Genesis, God saw the earth "filled with violence" before the flood (Genesis 6:11).

Other Jewish writings of the time also mention the giants. Jubilees retells the story. A scroll found at Qumran, called the *Book of Giants*, tells more about them. Heiser read these texts as evidence of how widely Jews in the Second Temple period knew the story.

words.d: in 1 Enoch 7, the children of the Watchers and human women; linked by the book to the Nephilim
an Aramaic writing found among the Dead Sea Scrolls that tells more about the giants of the Watchers story

look.title: The Earth Cries Out
look.text: Picture a long, still valley after a hard season. The fields are bare. The villages are quiet and worried. In 1 Enoch, it is as if the land itself raises its voice to heaven and asks for help.
look.prompt: 1 Enoch describes the earth as if it could cry out. What does this picture help readers understand about how the story sees the harm done?

check.q: According to 1 Enoch 7, who were the giants?
choices: The children of the Watchers and human women
check.why: 1 Enoch 7 says the Watchers' wives bore giants, linked to the Nephilim.

check.q: Which Qumran text tells more about the giants?
check.why: The Aramaic Book of Giants, found at Qumran, expands on the giants of the Watchers story.

check.q: What does Genesis 6:11 say the earth was filled with before the flood?
check.why: Genesis 6:11 says the earth was filled with violence, which 1 Enoch connects to the giants.

lessons.title: Four Angels Hear the Cry
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Enoch 9 the angels Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel see the harm on earth and bring the cry of the earth to God.
reading: 1 Enoch 9 turns to heaven. Four angels look down and see what is happening on the earth. Charles's translation names them Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel. They hear the cry of people and bring it before God. They say that God knows everything and ask what should be done.

Two of these names are in the Hebrew Bible. Michael appears in Daniel 10 and 12 as a great prince. Gabriel appears in Daniel 8 and 9 and again in Luke 1. Raphael appears in the book of Tobit, which is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Uriel appears in 1 Enoch and other Jewish writings.

In 1 Enoch these four are faithful angels. They stand in contrast to the Watchers who broke their oath to God's order. Heiser described the Bible's heavenly world as a *divine council*, God's heavenly family and court. In 1 Enoch, loyal and rebel members of that heavenly world are shown side by side.

words.d: a chief angel; Jude 9 calls Michael an archangel, and later tradition lists others
Heiser's term for God's heavenly family and court of spirit beings, as in Psalm 82 and 1 Kings 22
a Jewish book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles where the angel Raphael helps a family

look.title: Where the Four Angels' Names Appear
look.cite: Daniel 10:13, 12:1; Jude 9; Revelation 12:7; Daniel 8:16, 9:21; Luke 1:19, 26; Tobit 12:15; 1 Enoch 9:1 (Charles, 1917)
look.prompt: Which angel is named in the most books? Uriel is not in this table. Where does the reading say his name appears?

check.q: Which four angels bring the earth's cry to God in 1 Enoch 9?
check.why: 1 Enoch 9:1 names Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel.

check.q: Where does the angel Raphael appear in some Bibles?
check.why: Raphael appears in Tobit, which is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

check.q: What did Heiser mean by the divine council?
choices: The committee that chose the canon
God's heavenly family and court of spirit beings
check.why: Heiser used divine council for God's heavenly family, as seen in Psalm 82 and 1 Kings 22.

lessons.title: Bound Until Judgment
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Enoch 10 God sends angels to bind the Watchers in the earth until a final judgment, an idea echoed in 2 Peter and Jude.
reading: In 1 Enoch 10 God answers. An angel is sent to warn Noah that a flood is coming, so he can be kept safe. Raphael is told to bind Azazel and place him in darkness in the desert. Michael is told to bind Shemihazah and the others. They are held under the earth for seventy generations, until the day of *judgment*.

Gabriel is sent against the giants, and the book says they destroy one another. Then the earth is to be healed. The chapter looks ahead to a time when the earth is clean, people are righteous, and the land gives plenty. The tone moves from sorrow to hope.

The New Testament uses similar pictures. Jude 6 speaks of angels who did not keep their first place, held in chains until the great day. 2 Peter 2:4 says God put sinning angels in chains of darkness in Tartarus. Heiser argued these writers assumed their readers knew the Watchers story. Others think the writers simply shared common Jewish language.

words.d: in this story, God's final decision about right and wrong at the end of days
tied or held so as not to move freely; in 1 Enoch 10, the Watchers are bound under the earth

look.title: Three Texts, One Picture
look.text: 1 Enoch 10: Watchers bound in darkness under the earth until judgment. Jude 6: angels who left their proper home kept in chains under darkness until the great day. 2 Peter 2:4: angels who sinned put in chains of darkness in Tartarus, kept for judgment.
look.prompt: Which words or ideas repeat across all three texts? Does repeating an idea prove one writer read another? What else could explain it?

check.q: In 1 Enoch 10, which angel binds Azazel?
check.why: 1 Enoch 10 says Raphael is sent to bind Azazel and place him in darkness.

check.q: Which New Testament verse speaks of angels who left their proper place and are kept in chains?
check.why: Jude 6 speaks of angels who did not keep their first place, held in chains until the great day.

check.q: How does 1 Enoch 10 end its picture of judgment?
choices: With hope that the earth will be healed and give plenty
check.why: After the binding, 1 Enoch 10 looks ahead to a healed and fruitful earth.

lessons.title: Enoch the Go-Between
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Enoch 12–16 the Watchers ask Enoch to plead for them, and in a vision of heaven he learns their request is refused.
reading: In chapters 12–16, Enoch enters the story. The Watchers, now facing judgment, ask him to write a request to God for mercy. Enoch writes it. He goes to the waters of Dan, near Mount Hermon, reads it, and falls asleep. Then he has a *vision*.

In the vision Enoch is taken up to heaven. Chapter 14 describes a great house of fire and ice and a high throne. God speaks to Enoch. The answer is that the Watchers will have no peace. They were meant to live in heaven, but they left their place. Enoch must carry the answer back to them.

Here Enoch acts as an *intercessor*, someone who pleads for others. His request is refused. The scene shows the book's view that the Watchers' choice was very serious. It also shows Enoch as a trusted messenger who can stand near God's throne, which fits Genesis 5:24.

words.d: a sight or experience in which someone sees things beyond ordinary sight, often while dreaming
someone who asks or pleads on behalf of other people

look.title: A Message That Cannot Be Changed
look.text: Enoch sits by the waters of Dan with a scroll. He has written the Watchers' request carefully. He reads it aloud, then sleeps. When he wakes, he knows the answer, and it is not the one they hoped for. He goes to tell them.
look.prompt: Why might the writer place Enoch, a human, between the Watchers and God? What does this say about how the book sees Enoch?

check.q: What do the Watchers ask Enoch to do?
choices: Write and present a request to God for mercy
check.why: In 1 Enoch 13 the Watchers ask Enoch to write a request for mercy.

check.q: What answer does Enoch receive in his vision?
choices: The Watchers will have no peace
The Watchers will rule the earth
The Watchers may return to heaven
check.why: 1 Enoch 12–16 says their request is refused and they will have no peace.

check.q: What is an intercessor?
choices: Someone who pleads on behalf of others
check.why: Enoch acts as an intercessor when he presents the Watchers' request.

sections.title: Heiser and the Sages of Babylon

lessons.title: The Apkallu of Mesopotamia
lessons.mainIdea: Mesopotamian stories told of apkallu, wise beings who brought knowledge to people before the great flood.
reading: Long before 1 Enoch, people in Mesopotamia told stories about a great flood. Mesopotamia is the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in today's Iraq. Their stories also told of the *apkallu*. These were seven wise beings who lived before the flood. They were said to have taught people how to build cities and live in an orderly way.

In Mesopotamian art, apkallu often appear as men wearing fish-skin cloaks, or with bird heads and wings. A Babylonian priest named *Berossus*, writing in Greek around 290 BCE, described a fish-like teacher called Oannes. He said Oannes came up from the sea and taught people writing, farming and law.

Some Mesopotamian texts also say that after the flood, later sages were said to be partly human and partly apkallu. In those stories, wise beings and humans mixed. The apkallu were seen as sources of the knowledge that made kings great. Babylon's kings were proud of this heritage.

words.d: in Mesopotamian tradition, seven wise beings before the flood who were said to have taught people knowledge and skills
the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, mostly in today's Iraq, home of Sumer, Assyria and Babylon
a Babylonian priest who wrote a history of Babylon in Greek around 290 BCE

look.title: A Carving from Assyria
look.text: In many museums you can see Assyrian stone carvings from about 900–700 BCE. Some show tall figures with wings and bird heads, or men draped in a cloak shaped like a fish. Scholars identify many of these figures as apkallu, carved to guard palaces.
look.prompt: If a king placed apkallu carvings in his palace, what message might he be sending about where his power and wisdom came from?

check.q: Who were the apkallu in Mesopotamian tradition?
choices: Wise beings before the flood said to have taught people knowledge
check.why: Mesopotamian texts describe seven apkallu who brought knowledge before the flood.

check.q: Who was Berossus?
choices: A Babylonian priest who wrote about Oannes in Greek
check.why: Berossus wrote a history of Babylon in Greek around 290 BCE, describing Oannes.

check.q: Where was Mesopotamia?
choices: Between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers
check.why: Mesopotamia is the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, mostly in today's Iraq.

lessons.title: Genesis 6 as an Answer
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser argued that Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch answered Babylon's apkallu stories by treating those heavenly teachers as rebels, not heroes.
reading: In Reversing Hermon (2017), Heiser argued that Genesis 6:1–4 is a *polemic*, a text that argues against another view. He built on the work of other scholars, such as Amar Annus. They noticed that the Watchers story looks like the apkallu stories turned upside down.

In Babylon's stories, the apkallu were honored teachers who brought civilization. In 1 Enoch, heavenly beings also bring knowledge before the flood. But here they are rebels, and their teaching spreads harm. Heiser argued that Jewish writers, some of whom lived in exile in Babylon, were answering Babylon's pride. Babylon's great wisdom, in this reading, came from a rebellion.

Not every scholar agrees. Some think the similarities are loose or come from shared ancient ideas. Others focus on Greek or Canaanite parallels instead. Heiser also warned against modern claims that such stories describe aliens or giants who built pyramids. He said the right way to test any idea is to read the ancient texts carefully.

words.d: a text or argument written to challenge or answer another view
a similarity between two texts that may show a connection
being forced to live away from one's homeland; many Judeans lived in Babylon in the 500s BCE

look.title: Heiser's Argument in Brief
look.text: Heiser argued that Jewish writers knew Babylon's stories of wise beings who brought knowledge before the flood. They retold those events so that the heavenly teachers became rebels, and Babylon's proud learning became the result of a wrong choice.
look.cite: Michael S. Heiser, Reversing Hermon: Enoch, the Watchers, and the Forgotten Mission of Jesus Christ (2017), paraphrased
look.prompt: Put Heiser's argument in one sentence of your own. Then name one question a scholar who disagrees might ask him.

check.q: What is a polemic?
choices: A kind of ancient scroll jar
A text written to challenge another view
check.why: Heiser called Genesis 6:1–4 a polemic because he believed it answered Babylon's stories.

check.q: According to Heiser, how does 1 Enoch change the apkallu story?
choices: It makes the heavenly teachers into rebels whose teaching spreads harm
It makes the heavenly teachers into heroes
It moves the story to Egypt
check.why: Heiser argued the Watchers story turns Babylon's honored sages into rebels.

check.q: How did Heiser respond to claims that these stories describe aliens?
choices: He said aliens built the pyramids
He rejected them and said to test ideas against the ancient texts
check.why: Heiser rejected ancient-astronaut claims and urged careful reading of the texts.

review.q: Which passage in Genesis does the Book of the Watchers expand?
review.why: 1 Enoch 6–11 expands the brief story in Genesis 6:1–4.

review.q: What does 1 Enoch call the heavenly beings who came down?
review.why: 1 Enoch calls them Watchers; apkallu are the Mesopotamian sages.

review.q: On which mountain do the Watchers swear their oath?
review.why: 1 Enoch 6 places the oath on Mount Hermon.

review.q: Which Watcher teaches metalwork and weapon-making in 1 Enoch 8?
review.why: 1 Enoch 8 names Azazel as the teacher of metalwork, weapons and cosmetics.

review.q: What did Augustine and many later Christians think the sons of God were?
choices: Men from the family of Seth
review.why: The Sethite view reads the sons of God as men from Seth's line.

review.q: In 1 Enoch 12–16, what happens when Enoch presents the Watchers' request?
choices: In a vision he learns it is refused
review.why: Enoch's vision in 1 Enoch 14–16 brings the answer that the Watchers will have no peace.

review.q: Which Mesopotamian beings did Heiser compare with the Watchers?
choices: The apkallu, wise beings before the flood
review.why: Heiser argued the Watchers story answers Babylon's stories of the apkallu.

review.q: Which New Testament verses speak of angels held in chains until judgment?
review.why: Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 describe angels kept in chains for judgment, like 1 Enoch 10.
